title: Technology lock-in and substitution risk: Africa’s hidden green industrialization threat
body:
Africa is blessed with critical minerals for the green transition—cobalt, lithium, nickel, rare earths etc.

But here’s a hard truth: the biggest risk for resource-rich countries is not running out of minerals—it’s running out of relevance.

Why? Because technologies evolve—and they evolve fast.

- Today’s mineral may underpin tomorrow’s battery technology.
- But new chemistries, substitutes, or recycling breakthroughs can shift demand away from raw extraction.
- Countries stuck at extraction or basic processing are price-takers, vulnerable to global shifts.

Resources are not inherently valuable—they become valuable depending on what you do with them. Shukuru Amos pens a nice exposé on this (see https://lnkd.in/eFwGRx3H)

This is where end-to-end value chains are critical.

- Countries that move up the value chain—from extraction to processing, manufacturing, assembly, and even recycling—capture value at each stage.
- They build skills, know-how, and industrial capability that can adapt as technology shifts.
- They are not just exporting minerals—they are producing the technologies of the future.

Take batteries as an example:

- A country supplying lithium ore benefits only while demand for raw lithium is high.
- A country that produces battery-grade chemicals, assembles cells, and integrates storage systems locks in relevance across technological generations.

The message is clear:

- African countries cannot afford to think linearly—extract → export.
- They must think holistically—resources → value chains → capabilities → adaptation.

Timing matters. The window of opportunity is finite.

- Countries that fail to move quickly risk watching their minerals become obsolete in global markets while others capture the profits, skills, and industrial learning.

Africa’s green industrialization is therefore not just about minerals—it’s about strategic foresight, coordination, and industrial ambition.

The policy challenge is simple but urgent:

- Build end-to-end value chains, not just extraction or basic processing.
- Coordinate regional demand through mechanisms like AfCFTA.
- Invest in skills and technology learning that anticipate the next generation of green technologies.

In the green economy, relevance is more valuable than raw resources.

Elvis K. Avenyo (Ph.D.) Solomon Owusu Woubet Kassa, PhD Rex Asiama (PhD) Hubert Nii-Aponsah, PhD Emmanuel Buadi Mensah Victor Osei Kwadwo, Ph.D.
